overview: New Spain was a Spanish viceroyalty ruled from Mexico City from 1535 until independence in 1821. Its territory at different times stretched beyond present-day Mexico to parts of Central America, the Caribbean, North America and the Philippines. This vast colonial map contained many Indigenous nations, Africans, Europeans and mixed communities, not one uniform people. Coerced labor and epidemics caused great harm, while Indigenous officials defended land, Nahua students produced bilingual history, and craftspeople carried ideas across the Pacific. The imported border ends around 1715, well before the political end in 1821.

periods.title: Founding and early upheaval
periods.summary: The Crown organized a viceroyalty after conquest; Native communities faced epidemic disease and coerced labor while defending rights and preserving knowledge.

periods.title: Multilingual colonial society
periods.summary: Nahuatl and Spanish writing, Indigenous petitions, schools and medicinal gardens existed inside unequal colonial institutions.

periods.title: Pacific trade and local craft
periods.summary: Silver, Asian silk and porcelain moved through Acapulco, while artisans and families developed distinctive foods and art.

periods.title: Reforms and urban life
periods.summary: Art schools, public baths and varied family households show an active, unequal late-colonial society.

periods.title: War and independence
periods.summary: Independence fighting lasted more than a decade; Mexico inherited much, but not all, of the viceroyalty.

items.text: Spain created a viceroyalty in 1535, with its capital in Mexico City. At its greatest reach its jurisdiction included places far beyond modern Mexico. This imported polygon runs only from about 1530 to 1715 and cannot show every later border.
Conquest, disease and forced labor devastated many Indigenous communities. Their children and descendants remained, however, keeping languages, farming and legal claims alive under colonial rule.

A 1571 codex records Nahuatl officials complaining about mistreatment and underpayment by a Spanish administrator. It is a good reminder that Indigenous people argued in court and made records; they were not silent figures in somebody else’s history.

New Spain included Indigenous, Spanish, African and mixed communities with very unequal power. Later casta paintings tried to sort families into ranked categories; the pictures were an artist’s and patron’s scheme, not a complete portrait of how every family lived.

Nahua students helped make the Florentine Codex, writing Nahuatl in Latin letters beside Spanish translation and their own images. It preserved knowledge of food, plants and social life even while colonial authorities pursued conversion.

At Tepotzotlán, a Jesuit college taught some Indigenous boys and later elite students. Another school trained missionaries in Native languages. A child’s chance to study depended strongly on identity, place, family and gender.

The Royal Academy of San Carlos, founded in 1783, taught drawing and art. New Spanish artists also made portraits, city views and paintings for churches, using European, Indigenous and Asian-influenced traditions.

The Manila galleon brought Chinese silk and porcelain to Acapulco and carried American silver across the Pacific. A decorated dish in a New Spanish home could therefore tell a story that crossed oceans.

An eighteenth-century kitchen could contain turkey, pork, chile, cheeses and fruit preserves. Chocolate was popular across social groups. The mix of ingredients is much more interesting than a claim that everybody ate one “colonial meal.”

At the Tepotzotlán college, a botica stored medicines while the infirmary garden grew medicinal plants. Jesuits studied Indigenous healing knowledge as well as treating the sick. That was one institution; most families’ care varied widely.

Mexico City’s viceroy issued a 1793 rule for public baths and temazcales, including separate facilities and signs for men and women. The rule says poorer residents especially used the steam baths. So yes, a colonial government spent ink on bathhouse signs.

A small sample of official written Spanish is “baño y temazcal para mujeres,” meaning “bath and steam bath for women.” The 1793 ordinance required such lettering on a permanent sign; it shows how a written rule met an everyday door.

The colonial museum’s kitchen, refectory, pharmacy and convent rooms help imagine one institutional household. A mining family, Indigenous village or port neighborhood could look very different, so no single museum room stands for all New Spain.

Independence fighting began in 1810 and lasted through different leaders and factions until 1821. The end of Spanish viceregal rule was a long and violent political transition, not the end of the people living there.

Independent Mexico inherited most of New Spain in 1821, but not the Caribbean or the Philippines. Later borders changed again. The card’s 1715 map endpoint is especially easy to mistake for a fall date, so the historical ending is stated separately.

ending.text: The Spanish viceroyalty ended as Mexico gained independence in 1821. Mexico inherited most, but not all, of its territory; the Caribbean and Philippines had different futures. Indigenous and other communities continued despite colonial harm. The imported 1715 map endpoint marks a data snapshot, not the end of New Spain.

sources.title: INAH, Mexico: Greatness and Diversity, Colonial Society
sources.note: The Crown established a viceroyalty in 1535 after the 1521 conquest; Indigenous communities faced epidemics, coerced labor and imposed institutions but persisted.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Interwoven Globe timeline
sources.note: In 1535 the viceroyalty governed Mexico, Guatemala, the Caribbean, Florida and southwestern North America from Mexico City.

sources.note: Colonial legal records cover New Spain and later Mexican states, with historical jurisdiction extending well beyond modern Mexico.

sources.title: INAH, The 1576 cocoliztli epidemic
sources.note: Sixteenth-century epidemic diseases devastated Native communities and disrupted their societies.

sources.title: Library of Congress, San Salvador Huejotzingo Codex
sources.note: In 1571 Indigenous Nahuatl officials used a pictorial legal record to complain of mistreatment and underpayment.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Florentine Codex
sources.note: Nahua students wrote Nahuatl in Latin letters and painted illustrations; a Spanish translation stands beside their text.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Nahuatl as colonial lingua franca
sources.note: Priests and administrators used Nahuatl alongside Spanish in a multilingual colonial society.

sources.title: INAH, Jesuit pharmacy and health in New Spain
sources.note: At Tepotzotlán a botica stored remedies, and the infirmary garden grew medicinal plants; Jesuits studied Indigenous medicine.

sources.title: INAH, Museo Nacional del Virreinato
sources.note: Museum displays a pharmacy, infirmary garden, kitchen, refectory, convent women and the diverse late-colonial Mexico City plaza.

sources.title: INAH, Jesuits and education in New Spain
sources.note: The Tepotzotlán college taught Indigenous students and later elite students; educational access varied.

sources.title: INAH, Colonial kitchen in San Luis Potosí
sources.note: Recreated eighteenth-century kitchen includes turkey, pork, chile, milk, cheeses, jams and wood fire.

sources.title: INAH, New Spanish cooking and chocolate
sources.note: Colonial kitchens mixed charcoal cooking, Indigenous and Spanish vessels and widespread chocolate drinking.

sources.title: INAH, Mexico City bath and temazcal ordinance of 1793
sources.note: Viceroy regulated public baths and temazcales, including women’s and men’s facilities and permanent Spanish signs.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Painted in Mexico exhibition
sources.note: Eighteenth-century New Spain painting included portraits, devotional images, city views and casta pictures that idealized social categories.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Painted in Mexico exhibition galleries
sources.note: The Royal Academy of San Carlos was established in Mexico in 1783 and helped formalize artistic training.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Manila Galleon Trade
sources.note: Silver left New Spain for Asian goods; silk and porcelain came to Acapulco and influenced Mexican arts.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Independence from Spain
sources.note: Mexico achieved independence in 1821 and inherited most but not all of the viceroyalty; the Philippines and Caribbean were not part of independent Mexico.

sources.note: The war began in 1810 and ended in 1821 through different insurgent and royalist phases.
